summary: Belarus waives visas for citizens of 38 European countries — the whole EU, the UK, Switzerland, Norway and Iceland among them — for stays of up to 30 days (90 for Poland, Lithuania and Latvia) at any international road or rail crossing, under a regime that runs until December 31, 2026; CIS citizens and a list of bilateral partners enter visa-free, and a separate 30-day waiver covers 76 nationalities arriving and leaving through Minsk and five regional airports. US citizens and a few others can get a 30-day e-visa online; everyone else needs an embassy visa.

conflict.name: UK FCDO — Belarus entry requirements
conflict.states: Passport valid for at least 3 months from the date you arrive

travelInsurance.text: Medical insurance valid in Belarus with at least EUR 10,000 of cover is mandatory for foreign visitors — policies are checked at the border and can also be bought at entry points.

onwardTicket.text: Not required in itself. A ticket to your home country or a third country is one of the documents Belarus accepts as proof that you have enough money for the stay.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Belarus — rules of entry and exit for foreign citizens

proofOfFunds.text: Everyone entering must be able to show funds of at least 2 Belarusian base values for each day of a stay shorter than a month, or 50 base values for each month of a longer stay, counted at the rate on the day of entry. Cash in Belarusian rubles or convertible foreign currency, a document giving access to funds, prepaid accommodation and meals, a sponsor's letter of guarantee, or tickets home or onward all count.

source.name: State Border Committee of the Republic of Belarus — Border crossing rules for foreign citizens

currencyLimits.text: Cash over USD 10,000 (or the equivalent) must be declared in writing on arrival — Belarus applies Eurasian Economic Union customs rules.

source.name: State Customs Committee of the Republic of Belarus — Порядок перемещения наличных денежных средств и (или) денежных инструментов
source.instrument: Customs Code of the Eurasian Economic Union, Article 260(1)(7)–(8)

notes: Goods above the EAEU duty-free limits (EUR 500 and 25 kg when arriving by air) must be declared and duty paid.

payments.text: Cards are used everywhere by locals, but foreign-issued Visa and Mastercard often fail in Belarus because of sanctions on local banks. Bring cash in euros or dollars to exchange for roubles.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office advises against all travel to Belarus. The risks are political rather than street crime: anyone who has ever taken part in activity the Belarusian authorities now treat as illegal, including donations, faces a significant risk of arrest, laws are applied retroactively, and consular help is severely limited.

source.name: UK FCDO — Belarus travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: May to September is warm and green — best for Minsk, Brest fortress and the Belovezhskaya Pushcha national park; winters are long and cold.

idp.text: Belarus is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties

driving.text: Belarus is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Belarus yet.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

tips.text: Several Western governments currently advise against all travel to Belarus, citing the risk of arbitrary detention and the difficulty of providing consular help — weigh this carefully and tell your embassy if you go.

Do not count on land crossings: several Polish, Lithuanian and Latvian checkpoints are closed, lines at the open ones can run to many hours, and foreigners generally may not cross the Belarus–Russia land border at all. Arrive by air where possible.
Bring cash — foreign bank cards frequently do not work in Belarus because of sanctions, and exchanging euros or dollars for roubles is the reliable way to pay.
If you stay more than 10 days you must register with the local citizenship and migration office — hotels do it automatically, but private hosts often don't, and fines can be issued on departure.
Avoid photographing government buildings, police, military sites and border infrastructure. It can lead to questioning or detention.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Belarus?
faq.answer: It depends on your passport. Citizens of 38 European countries — the whole EU, the UK, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia and the European microstates — enter visa-free for up to 30 days (90 for Poland, Lithuania and Latvia, and no more than 90 days in a calendar year) at any international road or rail crossing until December 31, 2026, and CIS citizens and a list of bilateral partners are visa-free too. 76 nationalities (Canada, Japan, Australia and more) get 30 days visa-free only when flying in and out through Minsk National Airport or five regional airports. US, Bolivian and Paraguayan citizens can apply online for a 30-day e-visa. Everyone else needs a visa from a Belarusian embassy.

faq.question: Can EU citizens still enter Belarus visa-free?
faq.answer: Yes. The visa-waiver decree for European countries has been repeatedly extended and currently allows stays of up to 30 days (within a 90-day annual cap). It is a temporary measure, so confirm it is still in force close to your travel date.

faq.question: Can I enter Belarus overland from Russia?
faq.answer: Generally no. The Belarus–Russia land border has no international checkpoints for third-country nationals, so foreigners may not legally cross it by road or rail. Fly directly to Minsk or enter through another open border instead.

faq.question: Do foreign bank cards work in Belarus?
faq.answer: Often not — sanctions on Belarusian banks mean foreign-issued Visa and Mastercard frequently fail at terminals and ATMs. Bring enough cash in euros or dollars and exchange it for Belarusian roubles.

faq.question: Is travel insurance required for Belarus?
faq.answer: Yes — medical insurance valid in Belarus with at least EUR 10,000 of cover is mandatory for foreign visitors. It can be checked at the border, and local policies can be bought at entry points if yours does not qualify.

faq.question: Is it safe to visit Belarus?
faq.answer: Street crime is low and cities are orderly, but several Western governments advise against all travel because of the political environment — arbitrary detention is a real risk and consular assistance is very limited. Check your government's current advice before deciding.
